blocks.text: How do computers quickly find the greatest common divisor of two numbers? The answer lies in the ancient yet efficient Euclidean algorithm.

blocks.markdown: In this lesson, we will explore the concept of the greatest common divisor (GCD) and how to compute it using the Euclidean algorithm. We will also delve into the extended Euclidean algorithm to express the GCD as a linear combination of the original numbers, and learn how to find modular multiplicative inverses.

blocks.title: Greatest Common Divisor
blocks.text: The greatest common divisor (GCD) of two integers, $a$ and $b$, is the largest positive integer that divides both $a$ and $b$ without leaving a remainder.

blocks.markdown: The Euclidean algorithm is an efficient method for computing the GCD of two integers. It is based on the principle that the GCD of two numbers also divides their difference.

blocks.title: Finding GCD using the Euclidean Algorithm
blocks.prompt: Compute the GCD of 252 and 105 using the Euclidean algorithm.

steps.text: Step 4: The GCD is the last non-zero remainder.

blocks.title: Extended Euclidean Algorithm
blocks.text: The extended Euclidean algorithm not only computes the GCD of integers $a$ and $b$, but also finds integers $x$ and $y$ such that $ax + by = \text{gcd}(a, b)$.

blocks.title: Using the Extended Euclidean Algorithm
blocks.prompt: Use the extended Euclidean algorithm to express the GCD of 252 and 105 as a linear combination.

steps.text: Step 1: Record the steps of the Euclidean algorithm.
Step 2: Express each remainder as a linear combination.
Step 3: Substitute back to express 21 in terms of 252 and 105.

blocks.answer: The GCD of 252 and 105 can be expressed as $5 \times 105 - 2 \times 252 = 21$.

blocks.markdown: The modular multiplicative inverse of an integer $a$ modulo $m$ is an integer $x$ such that $ax \equiv 1 \pmod{m}$. This inverse exists if and only if $a$ and $m$ are coprime, i.e., $\text{gcd}(a, m) = 1$.

blocks.title: Finding a Modular Multiplicative Inverse
blocks.prompt: Find the modular multiplicative inverse of 3 modulo 11.

steps.text: Step 1: Use the extended Euclidean algorithm to express 1 as a linear combination.
Step 2: Express 1 as a linear combination of 3 and 11.
Step 3: The coefficient of 3 is the modular inverse.

blocks.answer: The modular multiplicative inverse of 3 modulo 11 is 4.

blocks.title: Key Points
blocks.text: The Euclidean algorithm efficiently finds the GCD. The extended Euclidean algorithm expresses the GCD as a linear combination, which is useful for finding modular inverses.

points: The Euclidean algorithm finds the GCD by repeated division.
The extended Euclidean algorithm expresses the GCD as a linear combination.
Modular inverses exist when the GCD is 1.
